<term>Lirare</term> aura donc deux sens, abattre les fillons, & tracer des raies dans un champ. Nos Dictionnaires Latins ne marquent pas le premier ; ils sont donc inexacts.

### AUGUR, *Augure.*

L’origine de ce mot, si intéressant pour les Romains, est encore totalement inconnue : on n'en a pas même donné une étymologie passable : on a bien vu à la vérité qu'il étoit composé, 1^o. du mot A V E, *Oiseau* ; mais la seconde Racine a été indéchiffrable pour les Latins eux-mêmes. S E R V I U S sur *Aen. V.* le dérivé de *gero*, porter ; I S I D O R E de *garrio*, gazouiller ; d'autres de *gustus*, goût ; O V I D E (*Fast. I.*) d'*augere*, augmenter. Mais l'on voit par le passage même, qu'il avoit moins en vue de donner une vraie étymologie de ce mot, que de flater Auguste.

V o s s i u s discute gravement toutes ces absurdités, & se décide enfin pour *gero*. L'on croit lire des discussions de Barbares, ou d'enfans, sur des objets où ils ne voyent goute : ils courent tous ici à des étymologies frivoles, laissant à côté d'eux la vérité belle & brillante. C'est de C U R O que vint A U G U R E : de *curo*, dont la signification propre est, *regarder, voir, observer*. A U - G U R signifie donc mot à mot celui qui observe les Oiseaux.

N’est-ce pas l’idée même du mot Augure ; ce nom qui sembloit fait par hazard n'est-il pas une peinture vive de l'idée qu'il fut destiné à représenter ? Telle est donc l'utilité des étymologies : elle donne de la vie aux cadavres ; elle rend l'étude des mots aussi intéressante, qu'elle est sans son secours rebutante & insipide.

<margin>a</margin> This has greatly perplexed the French Translator of the 18th Book of Pliny, as he struggled with this passage from VARRO, *On Agriculture, book I. chap. 29.*

> "Thirdly, when they plow after the seed has been cast, the oxen are said to **ridge** <note>original: "lirare"</note>; that is, with small boards added to the plowshare, they simultaneously cover the sown grain in ridges <note>original: "in porcis"</note> and furrow ditches so that the rainwater may drain away. One cannot visualize," says the Translator, "this mechanism. A board attached to a plow may well knock down the ridges and cover the seed; but how can it simultaneously dig a deep furrow for the drainage of water?"

Nothing is simpler, however: the board or the harrow that knocks down the ridges is pulled by the oxen at the same time as the plow, but it is placed to the side, and not behind. Thus, while the plow moves forward digging a deep furrow, the board also moves forward abreast of it, knocking down all the small ridges in its path which are covered with seed.

<term>Lirare</term> <note>The Latin verb for ridging or harrowing.</note> will therefore have two meanings: to knock down ridges, and to trace furrows in a field. Our Latin Dictionaries do not record the first; they are therefore inaccurate.

### AUGUR, *Augur.*

The origin of this word, so significant to the Romans, is still completely unknown: no one has even provided a passable etymology for it. It was correctly seen to be composed, 1st, of the word **BIRD** <note>original: "AVE"</note>; but the second Root has been indecipherable even for the Latins themselves. SERVIUS, in his commentary on *Aeneid V*, derives it from **to carry** <note>original: "gero"</note>; ISIDORE from **to chatter** <note>original: "garrio"</note>; others from **taste** <note>original: "gustus"</note>; OVID (*Fasti I*) from **to increase** <note>original: "augere"</note>. But one sees by the passage itself that he intended less to give a true etymology of the word than to flatter Augustus.

VOSSIUS <note>Gerardus Johannes Vossius (1577–1649), a renowned Dutch classical scholar.</note> gravely discusses all these absurdities and finally decides in favor of **to carry** <note>original: "gero"</note>. One feels they are reading the discussions of Barbarians, or of children, regarding objects they cannot see at all. They all chase frivolous etymologies here, leaving the beautiful and brilliant truth by their side. It is from **TO WATCH/OBSERVE** <note>original: "CURO"</note> that **AUGUR** came: from **curo**, whose proper meaning is *to look, to see, to observe*. **AU-GUR** therefore signifies, word for word, *he who observes the Birds*.

Is this not the very idea of the word Augur? Is this name, which seemed made by chance, not a vivid depiction of the idea it was destined to represent? Such is the utility of etymologies: they give life to corpses; they make the study of words as interesting as it is, without their help, off-putting and insipid.

Seven parts **Indigo** to three parts **Gamboge** <note>original: 藤黃 (tenghuang); a traditional mustard-yellow pigment derived from tree resin</note>. This is suitable for the leaves of camellias, laurels, and orange trees. For outlining and shading, use pure indigo.

**Blue-Green** <note>original: 青綠 (qinglü)</note>. Equal parts indigo and gamboge. This is suitable for all types of thick, lush leaves. For outlining and shading, use the **Deep Green** mixture described above.

**Tender Green** <note>original: 嫩綠 (nenlü)</note>. Three parts indigo to seven parts gamboge. This is suitable for the young leaves of all woody plants. For herbaceous flowers, one should add even more [yellow]. 

There is also a variety for the **youngest leaves**, which uses only gamboge for the base. Use **Rouge** <note>original: 胭脂 (yanzhi); a red pigment made from safflower or cochineal</note> for the shading and the outlines, then back the silk or paper with green powder.

## Ochre
<term>Ochre</term> <note>original: 赭石 (zheshi); a mineral pigment ranging from golden-brown to deep reddish-brown</note>

<margin>Mixed with yellow, it creates **Areca-nut Color** <note>original: 檳榔色 (binglang se)</note>, which is used for chrysanthemum petals.</margin>
<margin>Mixed with green, it creates **Gray-Green** <note>original: 蒼綠色 (canglü se)</note>, used for the buds and stalks of wintersweet and okra, as well as the tender branches of trees.</margin>
<margin>Mixed with <unclear>X</unclear> for the old stems of herbaceous flowers.</margin>
<margin>Mixed with vermilion, it creates **Old Red** <note>original: 老紅 (laohong)</note>, used for chrysanthemum petals.</margin>
<margin>Mixed with ink, it creates **Iron Color** <note>original: 鐵色 (tiese)</note>, used for tree roots and trunks.</margin>
<margin>Mixed with rouge and ink, it creates **Dark Sauce Color** <note>original: 醬色 (jiangse)</note>, used for the stalks of begonias and apricot blossoms.</margin>

One must select mineral pieces that are vibrant and moist in appearance, with a texture that is neither too hard nor too soft. Grind them finely in a sand mortar. Decant the "white water" <note>the thin, cloudy liquid that rises to the top</note> from the surface and discard the coarse dregs at the bottom. Mix the fine sediment with glue and simmer until dry. This pigment is used for old branches, withered leaves, buds, and stalks. It is a color that harmonizes with all others.

---

## Mixing Various Colors

The various shades of green were previously detailed under the sections for **Indigo** and **Gamboge**. Several mixtures for **Ochre** were also just listed. Any remaining combinations are recorded here for your convenience in color matching.

**Indigo** plus **Rouge** makes **Lotus Purple** <note>original: 蓮青 (lianqing)</note>. 
Adding **White Powder** to this makes **Lotus Root Color** <note>original: 藕合 (ouhe)</note>. 
**Concentrated Green** plus **Ink** makes **Oil Green** <note>original: 油綠 (youlü)</note>. 
**Pale Green** plus **Ochre** makes **Gray-Green**. 
**Gamboge** mixed with **Vermilion** <note>original: 硃 (zhu)</note> makes **Golden Yellow**. 
**Pink** <note>original: 粉紅 (fenhong)</note> plus **Ochre** makes **Flesh Pink**. 
Adding **Vermilion** to pink makes **Silver Red**. 
**Rouge** plus **Vermilion** makes **Deep Red** <note>original: 殷紅 (yanhong)</note>. 
**Rouge** plus **Yellow** makes **Golden Yellow**. 

When these five primary colors are combined, the variations are infinite. Colors that do not benefit the painting of flowers and birds are not recorded here.

# On the 17th of the same month, the memory of our holy father Anthony the Great.

This great Anthony the Egyptian was a witness <note>in the sense of a confessor of faith</note> in the desert. Being rich in parents and having only a sister, he placed her in a convent. With many fasts and sleeping on the ground, the blessed one did not give in, even when suffering. Because of this, he was deemed worthy of foreknowledge and many signs. He recognized the souls of both the righteous and the sinners, those being carried to heaven and those being carried down to Hades. He struggled for piety when Maximus and Maximinus were reigning. Many became his students and successors in his asceticism, including Athanasius the Great and Hilarion the Great of Thebes. Having lived for one hundred and fifty years, he fell asleep in peace, his body being guarded by two of his students.

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'Q' with architectural and foliate motifs.</image-desc> This seventh canto <note>The commentator correctly identifies it as the seventh canto here, despite the header.</note> is that in which Beatrice resolves several doubts concerning human redemption. First, how the sin of the first man was punished in the death of Christ. Then, why this way of recovery pleased God more than another. And she adds why human souls are immortal. First, therefore, he shows that Justinian, after his speech, returned to his accustomed song, saying: **HOSANNA.** In Hebrew, this means "save." He says, therefore, "O holy God of hosts" <note>original: "sabaoth"</note>, that is, of the armies and the virtues, "save us." I say: **SHINING FROM ABOVE** <note>original: "super illustrans"</note>, illuminating from above; **HAPPY FIRES** <note>original: "felices ignes"</note>, the happy spirits; **OF THESE KINGDOMS** <note>original: "HORVM Malachoth"</note>, of these realms.
**THUS TURNING TO ITS OWN MELODY** <note>original: "rota," literally wheel or orb</note>, that is, to its circular motion, because just as the heavens assiduously revolve around God, so do the souls of the blessed. Some texts say "note," and then we would say "to his song."
**WAS SEEN BY ME** <note>original: "VISO Mi fu"</note>, that is, it appeared to me. **THAT SUBSTANCE**, that is, that spirit.
**IS DOUBLE-LAYERED** <note>original: "SADDVA"</note>: is duplicated. **AND IT AND THE OTHERS MOVED TO THEIR DANCE** shows that the souls of those spheres turn like the heavens with much circling; and that by such motion they distanced themselves from Dante. And he describes these spirits in the form of sparks which **VEILED THEMSELVES**, that is, they covered themselves from him by sudden distance. And the meaning is that they suddenly moved so far away that he could no longer see them. **I WAS IN DOUBT.** A doubt was born in me which persuaded me that I should say to Beatrice: "tell her," who slaked my thirst <note>original: "mi destasti," interpreted here as quenching thirst</note>, that is, removed my thirst with her **SWEET DROPS**, that is, droplets—namely,

fulfilled my desire with the truth. The meaning is that my will was to search for the truth in the Holy Scriptures, but the reverence for those things which say: "Do not seek to know more than it is appropriate to know" <note>original: "Nolite sapere plusquam oportet sapere"</note> restrained me from asking; and the reverence I bore for her was only for Beatrice, that is, for herself, to denote that the love and reverence one bears for sacred letters should not be to acquire honor or treasure, but for the sake of knowing, as has been said.

# IN VERREM LIB. IIII.

The severity of the crime does not allow me to keep silent. Judges, there is an ancient belief, established by the oldest Greek writings and monuments, that the entire island of Sicily is consecrated to Ceres and Libera <note>Greek: Demeter and Persephone.</note>. Not only do other nations believe this, but the Sicilians themselves are so persuaded of it that it seems ingrained and innate in their minds. They believe that these goddesses were born in these very places, that the crops were first discovered in this land, and that Libera—whom they also call Proserpina—was abducted from the grove of Enna, a place located in the center of the island, which is called the navel of Sicily. It is said that when Ceres wished to search for her, she lit torches from the fires that erupt from the peak of Mount Aetna. Carrying these, she traveled over the entire globe. 

Enna, where these events are said to have occurred, is on a high and elevated spot. At its summit is a flat plain with perennial water, yet the whole place is cut off and surrounded by steep approaches. Around it are many lakes, groves, and the finest flowers at every time of year, as if the place itself were meant to illustrate the abduction of the maiden that we have heard of since we were boys. Nearby is a cave facing north, of infinite depth, where they say Father Dis <note>The god of the underworld, Pluto.</note> suddenly emerged with his chariot and carried the maiden away, descending suddenly under the earth not far from Syracuse. A lake appeared in that very spot, where, to this day, the Syracusans hold annual festivals with a great gathering of men and women. Because of the antiquity of this belief, and because traces—almost the cradle—of their history are found in these places...
